events.title: Publication of "Forty years of community-based forestry" (FAO Forestry Paper)
events.description: A review paper authored by Don Gilmour for the FAO that assesses the extent and effectiveness of community‑based forestry over a forty‑year period.
events.supporting_text:
Forty years of community-based forestry A review of its extent and effectiveness

FAO FORESTRY PAPER Don Gilmour

significance.justification: The publication disseminates knowledge about community‑based forestry, enabling stakeholders to act on the findings.
significance.supporting_text: Publication of "Forty years of community-based forestry" (FAO Forestry Paper)

events.title: FAO adopts the term “community forestry”
events.description: FAO formally introduced the umbrella term “community forestry” to denote any situation that intimately involves local people in forestry activities.
events.supporting_text: FAO (1978, p. 1) originally adopted the term "community forestry" as an umbrella term for "any situation which intimately involves local people in a forestry activity".

significance.justification: The adoption creates a common label that shapes discourse about community involvement in forests.
significance.supporting_text: FAO (1978, p. 1) originally adopted the term “community forestry” as an umbrella term…

events.title: FAO defines “social forestry”
events.description: FAO used the term “social forestry” (without a clear definition) to refer to a narrower set of activities such as establishment of woodlots for deforestation mitigation and fuelwood provision.
events.supporting_text: "Social forestry" is used by some as interchangeable with community forestry and by others to describe a much narrower spectrum of activities such as establishment of woodlots to address deforestation and provide fuelwood (FAO, 1991).

significance.justification: The definition is noted as vague, highlighting ongoing confusion about terminology.
significance.supporting_text: the concurrent emergence of the term “social forestry”, for which no clear definition exists, began a degree of confusion…

events.title: FAO defines “participatory forestry”
events.description: FAO provided a definition of participatory forestry as processes and mechanisms that enable stakeholders with a direct stake in forest resources to participate in decision‑making across all aspects of forest management.
events.supporting_text: FAO (2012b) has defined participatory forestry as: "processes and mechanisms which enable people with a direct stake in forest resources to be part of decision-making in all aspects of forest management, including policy formulation processes".

significance.justification: The definition explicitly enables stakeholder participation in forest decision‑making.

events.title: Menton & Cronkleton 2014 review of CBF initiatives in the Peruvian Amazon
events.description: Menton and Cronkleton published a review of community‑based forestry initiatives in the Peruvian Amazon, concluding that comprehensive assessments of programme effectiveness were lacking.

We couldn't find any comprehensive assessments of the effectiveness of existing programmes to promote community forestry or benefit local people."

events.description: FAO released the seminal paper that formally introduced community‑based forestry as a recognizable modality of forest management.
events.supporting_text: The emergence, growth and evolution of community-based forestry as a formally recognizable modality of forest management can be traced back to the seminal paper Forestry for local community development (FAO, 1978).

significance.supporting_text: The emergence ... can be traced back to the seminal paper Forestry for local community development (FAO, 1978).

events.title: Emergence of smallholder and community‑based forestry
events.description: During the 1970s and 1980s, smallholder and community‑based forestry emerged as a response to the perceived failure of the forest‑industry development model and rising rates of deforestation and forest land degradation in developing countries.
events.supporting_text: During the 1970s and 1980s, smallholder and community-based forestry emerged in response partly to a perceived failure of the forest industry development model to lead to socioeconomic development, and partly to the increasing rate of deforestation and forest land degradation in developing countries (Gilmour, King and Hobley, 1989).

significance.justification: Marks the start of organized community action to manage forests.
significance.supporting_text: During the 1970s and 1980s, smallholder and community‑based forestry emerged in response partly to a perceived failure of the forest industry development model.

events.title: Pilot projects testing Community-Based Forestry (CBF) modalities
events.description: During the 1980s, pilot projects were implemented in various settings to test community‑based forestry modalities as a response to large‑scale deforestation and environmental degradation, fostering people’s participation and bottom‑up development.
events.supporting_text: Pilot projects tested CBF modalities in different settings to address environmental concerns, Emergence of "people's participation" and bottom-up development

significance.justification: Pilots introduced participatory mechanisms that enabled community involvement in forest management.
significance.supporting_text: Pilot projects tested CBF modalities in different settings to address environmental concerns, Emergence of “people’s participation” and bottom-up development

events.title: Publication of Ostrom’s 1990 work on community‑based forestry
events.description: Ostrom’s 1990 publication popularised the narrative that local communities granted property rights can autonomously organise and sustainably manage forest commons, forming the conceptual basis for community‑based forestry.
events.supporting_text: The popularity of community-based forestry as a formal type of forestry rests primarily on a narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities, when granted sufficient property rights over local forest commons, can organize autonomously and develop local institutions to regulate the use of natural resources and manage them sustainably.

significance.justification: Introduces the narrative that local communities can self‑organize and manage forests sustainably, providing the conceptual basis for collective action.
significance.supporting_text: The popularity of community-based forestry ... rests primarily on a narrative popularized by Ostrom (1990) that local communities, when granted sufficient property rights ... can organize autonomously ...

events.title: Publication of Tole’s 2010 analysis of CBF within IMF/World Bank conditionality
events.description: Tole (2010) highlighted that community‑based forestry initiatives align with broader economy‑wide and institutional reforms promoted by IMF and World Bank conditionality lending since the 1990s, especially the downsizing of public service bureaucracies.
events.supporting_text: Tole (2010, p. 1312) noted that CBF initiatives "fit squarely within the larger economy wide and institutional reforms that many governments have been pursuing under IMF [International Monetary Fund] and World Bank conditionality lending since the 1990s. A significant condition in lending is that governments downsize their service bureaucracies in order to reduce costly public expenditures".

significance.justification: Shows how CBF is linked to broader IMF/World Bank conditionality and government cost‑cutting, highlighting external economic pressures.
significance.supporting_text: Tole (2010, p. 1312) noted that CBF initiatives “fit squarely within the larger economy wide and institutional reforms ... under IMF ... and World Bank conditionality ..."

events.supporting_text: The United Nations (UN) Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (adopted by the UN in 2007) has given additional impetus to this movement.

significance.justification: Gives additional legitimacy and momentum to the CBF movement by linking it to internationally recognised indigenous rights.
significance.supporting_text: The United Nations (UN) Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (adopted by the UN in 2007) has given additional impetus to this movement.

events.title: FAO’s 1991 review of community‑based forestry
events.description: FAO published a review of community‑based forestry, marking an early milestone in documenting the state of CBF programmes worldwide.
events.supporting_text: The two previous FAO reviews of CBF (FAO, 1991; Arnold, 2001) provide little in the way of quantitative or even qualitative data on the extent or effectiveness of community forestry.

events.title: Arnold’s 2001 review of community‑based forestry
events.description: Arnold (2001) reviewed 25 years of progress in community‑based forestry, calling for a shift from promotion to critical analysis and consolidation.
events.supporting_text: Arnold (2001), in reviewing progress with CBF over the previous 25 years, noted that "it could be desirable if there were now to be a period of consolidation, moving from promotion to critical analysis, with increased consideration of how best to address weaknesses and problems that have arisen".

events.title: Publication of Lawrence’s 2007 analysis of CBF evolution
events.description: Lawrence (2007) argued that community‑based forestry follows an evolutionary path from reductionist to systemic approaches, describing successive ‘generations’ of CBF development.
events.supporting_text: Lawrence (2007, p. 9) emphasized that CBF is not static. She argued that the evolutionary path of CBF "follows a trend from reductionist to systemic, from simple to complex and from planned to adaptive..."

significance.justification: Describes CBF’s transition toward systemic, adaptive management, indicating a trajectory for deeper transformation.
significance.supporting_text: Lawrence (2007, p. 9) emphasized that CBF is not static. She argued that the evolutionary path of CBF “follows a trend from reductionist to systemic ..."

events.title: Publication of McDermott & Schreckenberg’s 2009 comparative study of CBF regimes
events.description: McDermott and Schreckenberg (2009) highlighted distinct differences in how collaborative community‑based forestry regimes have evolved in the global North versus the global South.
events.supporting_text: McDermott and Schreckenberg (2009) noted distinct differences in the way that collaborative forms of CBF regimes have evolved in the global North and South.

events.title: Publication of Pokharel et al.’s 2008 study on Nepal’s community forestry
events.description: Pokharel et al. (2008) documented the evolution of Nepal’s community forestry from an environmental movement to a broader agenda encompassing gender, livelihoods, governance, and climate‑related issues.
events.supporting_text: As noted by Pokharel et al. (2008, p. 81), community forestry in Nepal "was initiated as part of an environmental movement, which aimed to conserve forests ... Later, it encompassed issues of gender, livelihoods and local institutional sustainability ... Most recently, governance, democracy and social inclusion have been brought into the ... agenda ..."

significance.justification: Shows how CBF can expand from pure conservation to broader social and governance objectives, indicating systemic evolution.
significance.supporting_text: Pokharel et al. (2008, p. 81), community forestry in Nepal “was initiated as part of an environmental movement ... Later, it encompassed issues of gender, livelihoods ..."

events.title: International PES Forum (2014)
events.description: A conclusion from an international Payment for Environmental Services (PES) forum held in 2014 noted that most PES schemes were small‑scale and had not met expectations for reducing tropical deforestation or providing additional income to forest owners.
